newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Mugabe marks 17 years in power in Zimbabwe.
newsitem.headline: Mugabe marks 17 years in power in Zimbabwe.

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe marks 17 years in power on Friday with his government on the defence against charges that it has become increasingly corrupt, arrogant and insensitive to public opinion.

"It's unfortunate that what people may remember most on independence day (April 18) is not that we have black majority rule, but that some people are on get-rich-quick schemes," said John Makumbe, an outspoken political scientist at Harare's University of Zimbabwe.
"There are so many things going on now and it's hard for political leaders to explain," he told Reuters.
The southern African country's social mood has been soured by the allegations that some government leaders and their cronies are plundering state coffers.

The government denies the charges, which have been fueled over the past month by its controversial decision to award a tender to establish the country's first private cellular phone network to a company in which Mugabe's nephew Leo Mugabe is a leading partner.
Many people had expected the tender to go to Strive Masiyiwa, a black Zimbabwean businessman whose Econet firm has been battling the state in courts for the last three years for such a licence.

The cellular phone tender was the third multi-million-dollar tender Leo Mugabe won in a row after he pocketed a contract to build a new international airport in Harare and another to treat sludge at the capital's main sewage works.
The president says he has never influenced the tender board to favour his nephew or anybody else, but his critics are sceptical.
Leading human rights groups, trade unions and private industry all charge that Mugabe has left open to abuse a programme aimed at economically empowering the country's black majority.

"Indigenisation of the Zimbabwean economy has been privatised, tribalised and monopolised by individuals from the ruling province or from the ruling family," said a statement by students issued during demonstrations last week against alleged corruption.

Besides the controversy over tenders, Mugabe has also been hit by charges that top state officials have been raiding a war victims' compensation fund set up for those wounded in a seven-year guerrilla war in the former Rhodesia that brought him to power in 1980.

Mugabe has ordered an investigation into the allegations and suspended payments, but some parliamentarians, including outspoken independent Margaret Dongo, still believe the president is soft on corruption and only moves in for damage-control.
His government also drew fire following disclosures that some of his senior cabinet colleagues had acquired farms meant to resettle landless peasants.

"High level corruption has eaten away at the social fabric of this nation and it has become imperative that remedial action be taken to bring this to an end," commented one of the country's leading financial newspapers, the Zimbabwe Independent.

"President Mugabe has been presented with another clear opportunity to send a clear signal to his colleagues and the public that now is the time for a clean government," it said of the war victims' compensation fund.

University of Zimbabwe's Makumbe and Kempton Makamure, a leading independent political activist, believe Mugabe is overwhelmed by these problems, which include unemployment estimated at over 40 percent.

Although Zimbabwe's economy rose by about eight percent last year and is forecast to grow by over five percent in 1997 following two successive good rainy seasons, many economic analysts say it will take time to recover from damage inflicted by Mugabe's 10-year socialist experiment in the 1980s.
"He has overstayed and probably doesn't know his way around. His main concern seems simply on staying on," Makamure says.
But Mugabe's aides say the president is, at 73, alert and in control and one of Africa's best leaders.
